The Week My Father Learned to Pay

The shutter was down and a printed notice was taped across it, one corner curling in the Bhagalpur heat. Papa read it the way he reads everything, with his thumb under the line and his lips moving a little.

"Band ho gaya," he said. Closed. Then, because that was not the part that worried him: "Passbook kaun bharega?"

Who will fill the passbook. For as long as I can remember, the answer was a man at counter two who stamped it, fed it to a machine that chattered like a sewing machine, and handed it back warm.

I had flown in from Bengaluru three days earlier with a laptop and a plan. The notice said his account had been moved to a branch on the far side of the city, two autos away. My plan was to put UPI on his phone so he would never have to go there. I build payment flows for a living. I have sat in meetings where grown adults argued about the shade of green on a Pay button. I thought this would take an afternoon.

What I did not say to anyone, including myself, was the other half of the plan. I wanted my father to be able to pay for things without me on the phone every time. And I was afraid he couldn't.

That evening, at the kitchen table, I installed the app, linked the account and set a PIN. "Four steps," I said. "Scan, amount, PIN, wait for the green tick." He nodded. He nodded the way he used to nod at my report cards, fully and without reading them.

I told him twice that the UPI PIN was a new one, not his ATM PIN. He nodded twice.

On Thursday we walked to the sabzi stall at the corner of our lane. The vendor's QR code was taped to his weighing scale in a plastic sleeve, its edges gone soft from monsoons. Papa had chosen palak and a handful of bhindi, and he was holding the phone at arm's length, as if it might go off.

He scanned. He typed the amount. He typed his PIN, and it was the ATM one.

The screen said what screens say. Payment failed. He tried again. Failed again. The third time the app told him to try after some time, a sentence I know the error code for, and I did not need the code to know what had happened. Behind us a woman with a cloth bag shifted her weight.

My hands were out before I decided anything. Papa turned his shoulder, the way he did when I was nine and tried to carry his bag.

"Rakho," the vendor said, not unkindly. "Kal de dena, Chacha."

Papa put the phone in his shirt pocket, the one that holds the pen, and said nothing until our gate. Then: "Pehle note nikalte the, gin lete the. Ab pata hi nahi chalta paisa gaya ki nahi."

Before, we took out notes and counted them. Now you can't tell whether the money went.

He was not talking about the app. For sixty-eight years money had been something he could count with his thumb. I had taught him four steps. There was a fifth, which no flow I have ever shipped includes: believing the money was still there when a screen said so.

That night we sent each other one rupee, again and again, across the table. My phone chirped each time: Received Rs 1 from Papa. Maa laughed from the kitchen at the sound. By the time she called us to dinner he had sent me eleven rupees and corrected his own PIN twice without a word from me. I had been teaching him the app. The real job was teaching him to trust it, and that is slower work, done in small sums.

On Saturday morning we went to the Hanuman mandir at the end of the lane. Panditji's steel thali sat next to the bell as it always does. Beside it, in a plastic sleeve, was a QR code, and next to that a small black speaker.

I stayed back with my hands in my pockets. Three days had taught me that much.

Papa took out the phone. He scanned. He typed 101, which is what you give a priest: a round sum and one rupee extra, so the blessing keeps going. He entered the PIN, the right one, and waited with the phone held steady, the way you hold a diya in a draught.

The speaker said, in a woman's voice, "Ek sau ek rupaye prapt hue."

Panditji touched his forehead. Papa laughed out loud, the real laugh, the one that closes his eyes. "Bhagwan ko bhi ab receipt milti hai," he said.

He did not look back at me. All week he had glanced at my face after every step, the way you check on the person holding the back of your bicycle seat. This time he did not check.

I think about that more than about the branch. A branch closing is a line in somebody's cost sheet, and I have written lines like it. I had not stood at the shutter. I had not seen what the line was made of: a counter, a stamp, a man who knew his name, a place where the paper told him the money was real. We design for a person with decent network, a new phone, patience and a child in the next room. My father had only the last of those, and only that week.

Most of us have a parent who nods when we explain. It took a shut shutter for me to hear that a nod can be a way of being polite to the person explaining.

I flew back on Sunday. The passbook was in my bag, because he had asked me to carry it in case the new branch needed it. The last entry was from March.

On Monday at 6:40 in the morning, my phone buzzed on the desk. Received Rs 1 from Papa. No message.

It was there again on Tuesday.

I have not asked him why. I send one rupee back.

# GST for D2C Brands in India: Registration, Marketplaces, Credit, Returns and Notices

A D2C brand that sells goods online in India needs four things in place for GST. The right registration. Invoices that match what it actually sold. Returns that agree with what its marketplaces and payment partners report. And someone who knows what to do the day a notice arrives. Most GST trouble for online sellers starts where two records disagree: what you reported, and what a marketplace reported about you.

This page is for D2C founders with annual revenue between Rs 1 crore and Rs 50 crore. It gives you the overview and sends you to [Firm name]'s detailed guide on each topic. It is general guidance, not advice on your own facts, and rates and limits change by notification, so check the date at the bottom.

## Jump to a section
1. The five-part GST routine
2. Registration: which GSTIN, in which state
3. GST on marketplace sales
4. Input tax credit
5. GST notices
6. E-invoicing
7. Returns calendar
8. TCS under GST
9. GST audits and GSTR-9C
10. Which route fits your brand (table)
11. FAQs

## The five-part GST routine
Every D2C brand, whatever its size, needs the same five habits.
1. Register in every state where you hold stock or are required to, not only your home state.
2. Invoice every sale, including returns, with the right HSN code and rate.
3. File GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B on time, then reconcile them with each marketplace's reports.
4. Claim credit only on purchases that appear in your GSTR-2B and are not blocked.
5. Keep a notice-ready file: invoices, settlement reports, credit notes and reconciliations by month.

## Registration: which GSTIN, in which state
Registration is state-wise, but the turnover test is all-India. A goods seller must register once aggregate turnover across all channels crosses Rs 40 lakh in a financial year (the limit is lower in some special-category states). It is not Rs 40 lakh per state or per marketplace.

Two things pull a D2C brand in earlier. Selling through a marketplace that collects TCS generally requires registration whatever your turnover, with a narrow exception for small intra-state goods sellers. And stock sitting in a marketplace warehouse in another state needs a registration in that state, which founders often discover only when the marketplace asks for a GSTIN to open the warehouse.

[Case A, anonymised D2C brand: one line on a registration gap the firm found and the figure it involved, supplied by the firm.]

Read the full guide: [GST registration for D2C brands: thresholds, states and warehouses](URL of cluster post 1).

## GST on marketplace sales
On an Amazon, Flipkart or Myntra sale, you are the supplier and the marketplace is the e-commerce operator. The sale is yours, so the tax on the goods is yours to report, even if the marketplace generates the invoice. The marketplace's commission, fulfilment and ad fees are separate services it bills you with GST, and you can claim credit on them.

Three records must agree every month: your GSTR-1, the marketplace's settlement report, and the TCS the marketplace files about you. Customer returns and RTOs need credit notes, and credit notes have their own deadline: 30 November after the financial year in which the sale was made.

[Case B, anonymised: a reconciliation gap between a seller's GSTR-1 and a marketplace report, with the amount, supplied by the firm.]

Read the full guide: [GST on marketplace sales: invoices, returns and credit notes](URL of cluster post 3).

## Input tax credit
Input tax credit lets you subtract the GST you paid on business purchases from the GST you collected. For a D2C brand the main credit lines are packaging, courier and logistics, marketplace fees, ad services and contract manufacturing.

Credit is allowed only when the supplier has filed their return and the invoice shows in your GSTR-2B. You also have a deadline: 30 November after the financial year in which the invoice was issued. Some purchases are blocked altogether. Goods you give away as gifts or free samples, which includes much influencer seeding, cannot carry credit.

Read the full guide: [Input tax credit for D2C brands: what you can claim and how to match it](URL of cluster post 4).

## GST notices
Notices come in a handful of forms, and the form tells you how serious the matter is. An ASMT-10 asks you to explain a mismatch found in your returns, with 30 days to reply unless extended. A GSTR-3A is a reminder for a missing return. A DRC-01 is a show cause notice that proposes a demand of tax, interest and penalty. Before a show cause notice, an officer may send an intimation in DRC-01A, and paying the tax and interest at that stage can close the matter.

What to do first:
1. Open the notice on the GST portal and note the form, the period and the reply date.
2. Find the mismatch it refers to: GSTR-1 against 3B, 3B against 2B, or your sales against TCS.
3. Do not ignore it. An unanswered notice becomes an order based on the officer's version of the facts.
4. Reply with documents, not arguments, and keep proof of what you filed.

[Case C, anonymised: one line on a notice resolved, the form, the amount at stake and the result, supplied by the firm.]

Read the full guide: [GST notices for D2C brands: ASMT-10, DRC-01 and how to reply](URL of cluster post 5).

## E-invoicing
E-invoicing is mandatory only for businesses above a turnover limit that the government has lowered in steps, and it applies to business-to-business invoices and exports, not to sales to consumers. A brand that sells only to consumers may never need it. A brand that adds wholesale, corporate gifting or distributor sales can cross the line without noticing.

[OUTLINE, about 200 words to be written: (a) the current turnover limit and the date it took effect. (b) Which of a D2C brand's invoices need an IRN and which do not. (c) What happens to a B2B invoice raised without one. (d) One client case on a brand that started wholesale mid-year.]

Read the full guide: [E-invoicing for D2C brands: who needs it and who does not](URL of cluster post 2).

## Returns calendar
Two returns carry most of the weight. GSTR-1 reports what you sold and is due on the 11th of the next month. GSTR-3B summarises the tax, carries the payment and is due on the 20th. Brands with turnover up to Rs 5 crore can opt for the quarterly scheme (QRMP) and pay monthly through a challan.

[OUTLINE, about 200 words to be written: (a) a month-by-month calendar for monthly and QRMP filers. (b) The order to work in: reconcile, file GSTR-1, check GSTR-2B, file GSTR-3B. (c) Late fee and interest. (d) One rule of thumb from the firm's own filing desk.]

Read the full guide: [GST returns calendar for D2C brands: GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP dates](URL of cluster post 6).

## TCS under GST
When you sell through a marketplace, the marketplace holds back a small percentage of the net value of your taxable sales as tax collected at source and pays it to the government. It files this against your GSTIN, and it appears in your electronic cash ledger as credit you can use against your GST liability.

[OUTLINE, about 200 words to be written: (a) the current TCS rate and the date it was set. (b) How net value is worked out after returns. (c) The monthly check: marketplace TCS report against GSTR-1 against your ledger. (d) What a mismatch notice looks like.]

Read the full guide: [TCS under GST for marketplace sellers: how to reconcile it](URL of cluster post 7).

## GST audits and GSTR-9C
There are two kinds of audit conversation. The annual return, GSTR-9, is yours to file. Above a turnover limit it comes with a reconciliation statement, GSTR-9C, which you or your CA certify yourselves. Separately, a GST officer can audit you and will send a notice in form ADT-01 asking for records.

[OUTLINE, about 200 words to be written: (a) who must file GSTR-9 and GSTR-9C, with the limits. (b) The five reconciliations that usually fail: books against GSTR-3B, GSTR-3B against GSTR-2B, e-commerce sales against TCS, HSN rates, and credit notes. (c) The records an officer asks for first. (d) One client case.]

Read the full guide: [GST audits and GSTR-9C for D2C brands: what to keep ready](URL of cluster post 8).

## Which route fits your brand
Use this table to see where a D2C brand lands before you read the detailed guides.

| | Regular registration | Composition scheme | Not registered |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who it fits | Most online sellers | Small traders with no inter-state or marketplace sales | Goods sellers below the threshold, selling within one state, outside marketplaces |
| Sell to customers in other states | Yes | No | Only where an exemption applies |
| Sell through Amazon, Flipkart or Myntra | Yes | No | Generally no |
| Claim input tax credit | Yes | No | No |
| Main catch | Monthly or quarterly returns and reconciliations | Rarely suits a brand that sells online | Easy to cross the line without noticing |

Most D2C brands end up in the first column. If you are unsure, the registration section above gives the test.

## FAQs

**Do I need GST registration to sell on Amazon or Flipkart?**
Generally yes, whatever your turnover. A marketplace that collects TCS expects a GSTIN from its sellers, and the exception for small intra-state goods sellers is narrow. Check yours against the registration guide.

**Can a D2C brand use the composition scheme?**
Usually not. Composition is closed to anyone making inter-state supplies of goods and to anyone selling through an e-commerce operator that collects TCS. A brand shipping across states or listing on a marketplace is out.

**I got a GST notice. What do I do first?**
Note the form, the period and the reply date, then find the mismatch it refers to. Do not ignore it, and do not pay before you know why the amount was raised. A CA can usually tell from the form which of your returns is being questioned.

**What is the difference between ASMT-10 and DRC-01?**
ASMT-10 asks you to explain a discrepancy found in your returns. DRC-01 is a show cause notice proposing a demand for tax, interest and penalty. The second is more serious and leads to a hearing.

**Why does my GSTR-1 not match what the marketplace reported?**
The usual causes are returns and cancellations booked in different months, TCS calculated on a different net value, and invoices raised by the marketplace on your behalf with a different date. The monthly reconciliation in the marketplace guide catches all three.

**What happens if I miss a return?**
You pay a late fee for each day of delay, up to the limit set by law, and interest at 18% a year on tax paid late. Missing returns for several periods can also lead to a registration cancellation notice.

## Next step
Not sure which of these sections you are exposed on? [Book a 15-minute GST health-check call](URL of booking page) and we will tell you where to look first.

Written by [Reviewer name], Chartered Accountant, [Firm name], Jaipur. Last reviewed [date]. We update this page when a linked guide changes.

EPISODE RUN SHEET: [Show name], Lucknow startup community
Guest: [Guest name], founder of [Brand], a chikankari D2C brand. Moved from wholesale to selling on Instagram in 2022.
Format: Hinglish video interview, 35-40 minutes. Host: [Host name].
Audience: small-town founders, 22-35.
Promise of the episode: what actually changed, week by week, when a chikankari maker stopped selling to shops and started selling to the person who wears it.
Before recording: read [Guest]'s own posts and past interviews. Pull three lines they have said before and one question they have probably not been asked. Put them where marked RESEARCH below.

TIMING (about 36 minutes)
Cold open 0:30
Intro 1:00
Guest intro 1:00
Segment 1: 8:00
Segment 2: 12:00
Mid-roll: 1:00
Segment 3: 10:00
Close: 2:00
Outro: 0:30

1. COLD OPEN (0:30, cut after recording)
Use the best 20-40 seconds of the guest's answer to Q1.3 or Q2.2, whichever is stronger. Mark it in the edit.
Fallback if neither lands, host line, recorded after the interview: "2022 mein ek chikankari founder ne wholesale chhodkar seedha Instagram pe bechna shuru kiya. Hum puchenge: kya toota, kya bacha, aur kya aap Lucknow se kar sakte ho."

2. INTRO (1:00)
"Namaste, aap sun rahe ho [Show name], Lucknow ke startup founders ki baatcheet. Main [Host name]. Aaj ka episode un logon ke liye hai jo shehar chhote hain, par kaam bada karna chahte hain. Aaj hum samjhenge ki wholesale se retail pe jaana asal mein kaisa hota hai, kisi pitch deck mein nahi, ek dukaan, ek Instagram page aur kuch karigaron ke beech."

3. GUEST INTRO (1:00)
"Hamare saath hain [Guest name], [Brand] ki founder. [Brand] chikankari ka D2C brand hai. 2022 mein inhone wholesale se Instagram selling pe switch kiya. [RESEARCH: one concrete, checked fact from their own page or press, e.g. a first product, a city, a milestone they have stated publicly]. Swagat hai."

4. SEGMENT 1: THE WHOLESALE YEARS (8:00)
Goal: the listener understands why a working wholesale business was worth leaving.
Q1.1 Wholesale ke zamane mein ek normal din kaisa hota tha? Subah se shaam tak batayiye.
  Follow-up: Aapke buyers kaun the, aur unse baat kaise hoti thi?
Q1.2 Wholesale mein sabse zyada kya acha tha, jo aaj aap miss karte ho?
  Follow-up: Aur kya cheez thi jo bilkul nahi chal rahi thi?
Q1.3 Wo kaunsa moment tha jab laga ki ab seedha customer ko bechna hai? Us hafte kya hua tha?
  Follow-up: Us din ke baad pehla kaam kya kiya?
  [CLIP 1, about 08:00: the turning-point answer. 45-60 seconds, vertical cut, Hinglish caption. Cut to start on the first sentence of the story, not on the question.]
Q1.4 Ghar mein aur karigaron ke saath is faisle pe kaisi baat hui?
  Follow-up: Kisi ne kuch aisa kaha jo aapko aaj bhi yaad hai?
Q1.5 Wholesale chhodne ka sabse bada risk aapko kya laga?
  Follow-up: Wo risk sach hua ya nahi?
Listen for: a specific day, a specific buyer, a specific sentence. If the answers stay general, ask "Ek example dijiye" before moving on.
If the guest runs short, spare question: Wholesale ke buyers ko Instagram pe jaane ki baat kaise batayi?
Transition: "Toh faisla ho gaya. Ab dekhte hain ki pehle mahine mein asal mein kya hua."

5. SEGMENT 2: THE INSTAGRAM SWITCH, 2022 (12:00)
Goal: leave the listener with specific moves they could copy in their own town.
Q2.1 Pehla order Instagram se kaun sa aaya, aur kahan se?
  Follow-up: Aapne us customer ko kaise sambhala?
Q2.2 Wholesale rate se retail rate pe aate waqt price kaise tay kiya?
  Follow-up: Kisi ne kaha ki mehnga hai? Aapne kya jawab diya?
  [CLIP 2, about 16:00: the pricing answer. 45-60 seconds. Keep the number or rule of thumb on screen as text, but only if the guest says it on the record.]
Q2.3 Content mein kya kaam kiya, aur kya bilkul nahi chala?
  Follow-up: Ek post ya reel jo aapko aaj bhi yaad hai, uske baare mein batayiye.
Q2.4 DM se order lena, payment, courier, return: in sabme se sabse zyada sar dard kaun sa tha?
  Follow-up: Aaj uska system kya hai?
Q2.5 Chikankari mein size, rang ya finish ko lekar customer ko expectation kaise set karte ho?
  Follow-up: Kabhi bada return ya complaint aaya? Kya seekha?
Q2.6 [RESEARCH: one question they have probably never been asked, built from their posts, e.g. about a product or a decision they mentioned only once.]
  Listen for: numbers the guest says on the record (price, timelines, order counts). Do not supply numbers yourself. If a number is new, ask "Ye figure public kar sakte hain?"
  If the guest runs short, spare question: Pehle 90 din mein sabse badi galti kaun si thi?
Transition into the break: "Yahan ek chhota sa break leke aate hain. Wapas aake baat karenge ki chhote shehar se ye sab kaise ho sakta hai."

6. MID-ROLL SLOT (1:00)
Place here, after Segment 2 ends and before the next question, at a natural pause.
Sponsor: [Sponsor name]. Read type: host-read, 60 seconds, three ranked talking points plus one mandatory line, supplied by the sponsor.
Host line in: "Break se pehle ek baat: ye episode [Sponsor name] ne sponsor kiya hai."
Host line out: "Toh wapas aate hain [Guest name] ke saath."

7. SEGMENT 3: FROM A SMALL TOWN (10:00)
Goal: the listener knows if this model fits them and what to try this week.
Q3.1 Lucknow jaise shehar mein ye model kisko suit karta hai, aur kisko nahi?
  Follow-up: Wholesale ko ek saath chhodna zaroori hai, ya dono chal sakte hain?
Q3.2 Maan lijiye koi 22-35 saal ka founder aaj ek hafte mein wholesale se retail test karna chahta hai. Wo kya karega?
  Follow-up: Pehla kharcha kahan jayega?
  [CLIP 3, about 29:00: the one-week test plan. 45-60 seconds. Open on "ek hafte mein". End the clip on the last step, not the thank-you.]
Q3.3 Karigar aur brand ka rishta kaise badla jab aap seedha customer ko bechne lage?
  Follow-up: Unhe aaj kya milta hai jo pehle nahi milta tha?
Q3.4 Wholesale se aapne kya seekha jo Instagram pe kaam aaya?
Q3.5 Aap kis cheez ko ab bhi nahi sulajha paaye hain?
  Follow-up: Us pe kisi se madad maangi hai?
Q3.6 Agar aap 2022 mein wapas ja paayein, to wholesale chhodne se pehle khud ko ek line mein kya salah denge?
  (Closing question. Always ask it last; the answer gives you the recap line.)

8. CLOSE (2:00)
Recap in one idea: "[One idea from the episode, in the guest's own words, picked while listening]."
"Shukriya [Guest name]. Aaj ki sabse kaam ki baat mujhe ye lagi: [recap line]."
Call to action, one only: "Agar episode kaam ka laga, to [Show name] ko [platform] pe follow kijiye, taaki agla episode seedha aapke paas aaye."

9. OUTRO (0:30)
"Ye the [Show name], Lucknow ke startup founders ki baatcheet. Guest ke vichaar unke apne hain. Agle episode mein hamare saath hain [next guest, if confirmed]. Milte hain."
Credits: [producer, editor, music].

EDIT NOTES
Chapters: one per segment plus the cold open, titled with the segment goal in plain Hinglish. Three clips marked above, each cut as its own vertical file.
Visual moments for the video cut: cut to the piece or post whenever the guest shows one. Show the product on screen during Q2.5. Leave the guest's face on screen for Q1.3 and Q3.6.
Cut anything from the mid-roll that is not the sponsor's mandatory line.

POLICY BRIEF

Ward-level heat action plans for Bihar's five Tier-2 cities: approve a one-season pilot

To: Principal Secretary, Urban Development and Housing Department, Government of Bihar; District Magistrates of [City 1], [City 2], [City 3], [City 4], [City 5]
From: [NGO name], Patna
Date: [date]
Decision requested: a decision meeting, within [30 days], on a one-season pilot of ward-level heat action plans.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Heat is a recurring risk in Bihar's cities. The response is organised at district level, while the harm lands ward by ward. Our data shows three things. Heatwave days averaged [X] a year across the five cities in 2019-2025 (IMD). The five district hospitals recorded [N] heatstroke admissions in 2025 (district hospital records). And wards differ widely: in a 12-ward survey, [Y] of 12 reported [finding, for example no public drinking-water point nearby] (our pilot survey, [month year], n = [N] households).

We recommend that the department approve a one-season pilot in the five cities. Each of [N] priority wards gets a heat action plan, a named coordinator, a trigger linked to the IMD alert, cooling and water points, and a standard heatstroke admissions record at the district hospital. The estimated cost is Rs [X] crore from [budget line to be confirmed by the department]. Success is measured by comparing admissions in pilot wards against the 2019-2025 baseline and against non-pilot wards. We ask for a decision meeting to approve scope, budget and nodal officers before the April-June season.

CONTEXT: WHY WARD LEVEL, WHY NOW
Heat risk is not spread evenly across a city. Our figures, with their sources:
- Heatwave days: [X] a year on average across the five cities, 2019-2025 (IMD station data for each city).
- Heatstroke admissions: [N] in 2025, up from [M] in 2019 (district hospital records, five district hospitals).
- Ward variation: in the 12 surveyed wards, [finding 1] and [finding 2] (our pilot survey, [month year], n = [N]).

What the figures show, in our reading: the heatwave threshold is a city-wide number. Who is hurt depends on housing, water access, outdoor work and distance to a hospital, which differ ward to ward. A district advisory reaches the ward only if someone in the ward acts on it. Today there is no named person in the ward whose job that is. [Department to confirm what plan or order is currently in force, so this paragraph can be made exact.]

What a ward heat action plan contains. We propose six parts, kept to one page per ward so a coordinator can use it:
1. A trigger: which IMD alert level starts which action in the ward.
2. A list of the ward's most exposed people and places: outdoor workers, older residents living alone, informal settlements, schools and anganwadis.
3. Cooling and drinking-water points, with their locations and opening hours.
4. A hospital link: the nearest facility, its heatstroke bed capacity and who the coordinator calls.
5. Messages in Hindi, sent through the channels the ward already uses, with advice on working hours and water.
6. A record: what was done on which day, so the season can be reviewed.

Who is affected. From the survey, the households with least protection are [group 1] and [group 2] ([Z]% and [W]% of surveyed households respectively, our pilot survey). We list them here because a ward-level plan is the first document that would reach these households by name. [Department to confirm whether current advisories already distinguish between wards.]

Ahmedabad's 2013 heat action plan and the NDMA's heat-wave guidelines are the usual reference points. This brief proposes testing a ward-level version in Bihar's own wards before any statewide commitment.

POLICY OPTIONS
| | A. Continue district-level advisories | B. Ward-level pilot in five cities (recommended) | C. One plan per city, no ward detail | D. Statewide rollout in all urban local bodies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| What it means | Alerts as today | [N] priority wards per city, one season, then review | One heat plan per municipal body | Ward plans everywhere at once |
| Cost estimate | Rs [X] crore (current spend, to be confirmed) | Rs [X] crore, one season | Rs [X] crore | Rs [X] crore |
| Who implements | District administration | Municipal body, ward coordinator, district hospital, district administration | Municipal body | All urban local bodies |
| Feasibility | Already in place | Fits the cities we have data for; needs nodal officers by [date] | Easy to notify, hard to verify | Capacity gaps in smaller bodies likely |
| Main trade-off | Does not reach the ward | Few wards; results after one season | Same blind spot as A | High cost; no Bihar evidence yet |

Our judgement, not a finding: B gives the department evidence from Bihar's own wards before it commits statewide money.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Approve a one-season ward heat action plan pilot in [City 1] to [City 5], starting with the 12 wards already surveyed and adding [N] more by [date]. Decision by: the department, at the proposed meeting.
2. Direct each municipal body to name a nodal officer and one coordinator per pilot ward by 28 February 2027, so plans are live before April. Instrument: a departmental order.
3. Link the IMD alert to a ward-level action trigger: coordinator informs the ward, opens the cooling and water points, and alerts the nearest hospital. Responsible: municipal body with the District Magistrate.
4. Set up [N] cooling and water points per priority ward, sited using the survey findings. Funding: Rs [X] crore from [budget line to be confirmed].
5. Introduce a standard heatstroke admissions record at the five district hospitals, noted by ward. Responsible: Health Department with the civil surgeons. Without ward-level admissions, no result can be measured.
6. Review at the end of the season by comparing pilot and non-pilot wards against the 2019-2025 baseline. [NGO name] will share the survey instrument and baseline data free of charge, and the department decides whether to extend, change or stop.

RISKS TO THE PILOT AND HOW WE WOULD HANDLE THEM
- Coordinator capacity: a ward coordinator may already hold other duties. We recommend a one-day briefing and a one-page plan template, and we will provide both.
- Data quality: heatstroke admissions are recorded unevenly. Recommendation 5 fixes the format before the season starts, and we will audit a sample of records in June.
- Cost: costs may rise if cooling points are built rather than designated. The pilot starts with existing buildings such as schools, community halls and ward offices where possible, and the costed plan shows both routes.
- Timing: orders after 28 February leave too little time before April. If the meeting is delayed, we propose starting with a smaller set of wards and adding more mid-season.

NEXT STEP
We request a decision meeting within [30 days]. We will bring the ward-level data, the draft order and a costed plan for each city, and we can present to the Principal Secretary and the District Magistrates in one session. Contact: [name, phone, email].

SOURCES
- IMD heatwave days, five city stations, 2019-2025: [source, document or station data reference].
- Heatstroke admissions, five district hospitals, 2019-2025: [source, office and year].
- [NGO name] 12-ward pilot survey, [month year], n = [N]: [link or annexure].
- NDMA, guidelines for preparation of action plans for prevention and management of heat wave: [edition, year to be confirmed before sending].
- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan, 2013: [document reference].

APPENDIX: SURVEY METHOD
[Method note supplied by the NGO: sampling of the 12 wards, number of households per ward, who collected the data, dates, questions asked, and limitations.]

samples.text:
[COMPANY] EMPLOYEE HANDBOOK, NOIDA

Policy 4.1: Hybrid Work and Attendance Policy
Policy 4.2: Prevention of Sexual Harassment (POSH) Policy, summary

Version: [1.0]
Effective date: [dd Month yyyy]
Owner: Head of People
Approved by: [name and role]
Next review: [date, 12 months after the effective date]
Status: DRAFT, marked for legal review.
HR and counsel must confirm the wording of Policy 4.2 before this is published.
Values in square brackets are proposals, not decisions. HR must confirm each one.

---

POLICY 4.1: HYBRID WORK AND ATTENDANCE

1. Purpose
This policy tells you how many days you must be in the Noida office, how to ask for an exception, and who to contact if something is unclear.

2. Scope
2.1 This policy applies to all employees and interns of [Company].
2.2 It applies to our two remote contractors only where their contract says so. Clauses 5.1 to 5.3 (availability) apply to them as written.
2.3 It does not cover leave, which is in the Leave Policy [reference].

3. Definitions
Office day (कार्यालय दिवस): a working day on which you work from the Noida office.
Remote day (घर से काम का दिन): a working day on which you work from your registered home address.
Core hours (कोर घंटे): the hours in which you must be reachable, whether in the office or remote.
Exception (अपवाद): approval to work differently from this policy on specific dates.
Manager (प्रबंधक): the person you report to for your day-to-day work.

4. Office days
4.1 You must work from the Noida office on [3] days a week.
4.2 The office days are [Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday] for all teams.
4.3 On the other [2] days you may work remotely from your registered address.
4.4 In a week with a public holiday, the number of office days is [reduced by 1].
4.5 Interns follow the same office days unless their offer letter says otherwise.
4.6 You must mark your attendance in [HR system] each day, whether you are in the office or remote.
4.7 You must get the Head of People's approval before you work from a city or country other than your registered address.
4.8 When you work remotely, you must use your company laptop and [VPN or approved connection] for company systems.
4.9 If your remote setup fails, for example a power cut or a broken connection, you must tell your manager as soon as you can and may move to the office for that day.

5. Availability
5.1 Core hours are [10:30 am to 4:30 pm IST] on every working day.
5.2 During core hours you must reply to messages and calls from your team within [30 minutes].
5.3 You must tell your manager before core hours begin if you cannot be reachable.

6. Exceptions
6.1 You may ask for an exception for specific dates, for example for a family event, a health need or a travel disruption.
6.2 Send the request on [form or channel] to your manager at least [2 working days] before the first date.
6.3 In an emergency, message your manager before core hours begin and send the form when you can.
6.4 Your manager will approve or decline within [2 working days] and will give the reason if the answer is no.
6.5 An exception longer than [5 consecutive working days] also needs approval from the Head of People.
6.6 The approval is recorded in [HR system] with the dates and the name of the approver.

7. Procedure to request an exception
1. Open [form or channel] and enter the dates and the reason in one or two lines.
2. Submit it to your manager.
3. Wait for the reply within [2 working days]. If there is none, send a reminder to [HR contact].
4. Check that the approval shows in [HR system] before the first date.

8. Roles and responsibilities
| Who | What they do |
|---|---|
| Employee | Follows the office days, marks attendance, asks for exceptions in advance |
| Manager | Decides exception requests on time and tells HR about patterns that need a conversation |
| Head of People | Owns this policy, decides long exceptions, reviews it every [12 months] |
| Intern | Follows clause 4.5; the offer letter decides any difference |
| Remote contractor | Follows clause 2.2 and the contract |

9. If the policy is not followed
9.1 If you miss an office day without an approved exception, your manager will speak to you within [5 working days] and listen to your reasons.
9.2 If it happens more than [3] times in a quarter, your manager will tell HR, and HR will meet you before any step under the Code of Conduct [reference].
9.3 If you disagree with a decision, write to [HR contact]. The Head of People will reply within [5 working days].

10. Related policies
Leave Policy [reference], Code of Conduct [reference], Policy 4.2 below.

11. Acknowledgement
I have read and understood Policy 4.1. Name: ____ Date: ____

---

POLICY 4.2: PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT (POSH), SUMMARY

This is a one-page summary of the full POSH Policy [reference]. The full policy and the law apply if there is any difference.

1. Our commitment
[Company] does not tolerate sexual harassment. Our policy follows the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. We have an Internal Committee (आंतरिक समिति) to receive and inquire into complaints.

2. Who is covered
All employees, interns, trainees and contractors who work with [Company], at the office, working remotely, in online meetings and chats, and on work trips. [Counsel to confirm the coverage for remote contractors.]

3. What counts as sexual harassment (यौन उत्पीड़न)
Unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature, direct or implied. Examples: physical contact or advances. A demand or request for sexual favours. Sexually coloured remarks. Showing pornography. Any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature.

4. How to complain
4.1 Write to the Internal Committee at [IC email address], or give a written complaint to the Presiding Officer.
4.2 You should complain within 3 months of the incident, or of the last incident if there were several. The Committee can extend this by up to 3 months if it records the reason.
4.3 If you cannot write the complaint, a Committee member will help you put it in writing.

5. What happens next
5.1 If you ask, the Committee may try conciliation before an inquiry. Conciliation cannot involve a money settlement.
5.2 The inquiry must be completed within 90 days. The Committee reports to [Company] within 10 days of finishing, and [Company] must act within 60 days of receiving the report.
5.3 The identity of the people involved, the complaint and the inquiry are confidential.
5.4 Retaliation against anyone who complains or gives evidence is not allowed and is treated as a separate breach.
5.5 [Company] will run POSH awareness sessions for all employees, interns and contractors [once a year] and will put the Committee's details on [intranet page].

6. Complaints from colleagues who are not women
The 2013 Act protects women. Colleagues of any gender can raise a complaint of harassment with the Head of People under the Code of Conduct. [Counsel to confirm this route.]

7. Internal Committee details
Presiding Officer: [name, email, phone]
Members: [name], [name]
External Member: [name, organisation]
IC email: [IC email address]
Escalation: [HR contact] and the Head of People, [email]

Acknowledgement: I have read and understood Policy 4.2. Name: ____ Date: ____

The Diwali film we made without a camera

A 30-second Diwali film for a regional jewellery brand, made in 10 days with no live shoot: [views] views and [saves] saves in the brand's own report.

SNAPSHOT
Role: art direction and the generation pipeline. I set the look, set the rules the team used to approve or reject a frame, and ran the pipeline from the first reference to the final export.
Team: 4 (me, plus [role], [role], [role])
Timeline: 10 days, brief to delivery
Client: regional jewellery brand (anonymised under NDA)
Tools: [generation, editing and sound tools]
Format: 30-second film, [aspect ratio and platform]

BRIEF AND CONSTRAINT
The brand needed a 30-second Diwali film. There would be no live shoot: no studio, no models, no jewellery in front of a lens. We had 10 days and four people.

That made the real problem narrow. Jewellery buyers notice a wrong clasp or a stone that has moved. AI-generated video is good at mood and weak at staying exact from frame to frame. The film had to carry the feeling of Diwali and still show the client's pieces correctly.

APPROACH
I treated the generator as a location and lighting department, and the product as fixed. Generation would build the world and the light. The jewellery would stay the client's, exactly as designed. [How the real pieces entered the film, in one line.]

KEY DECISIONS
1. Keep the product exact, let the world move.
Options: let the model design the pieces; use the client's own product images as a fixed reference; place real product images over generated scenes. Chosen: [her choice]. Why: a misdrawn piece costs a jewellery client's trust faster than a plain background costs attention. It also gave the team one simple review rule: any frame where a piece differed from the client's design was out, however good it looked.

2. Fewer, longer shots.
Options: about fifteen quick cuts, or five or six held shots. Chosen: [number] shots. Why: every cut is another chance for a piece to change shape, and ten days leave little time for redoing shots. Fewer shots meant each one could be checked properly, and the editor got longer clean clips to work with.

3. A human finish.
Options: deliver the generated clips as they came, or grade, time and score them by hand. Chosen: [her choice]. Why: generated clips arrive with slightly different colour and grain. One grade and one sound pass made them read as one film.

IMAGES AND CAPTIONS
1. Hero frame. Look at [the detail: for example the clasp or the stone setting] and how the warm light stays on the piece while the background moves.
2. The brief board. Three lines from the client's brief, with the no-shoot constraint circled.
3. The pipeline map. Each step from reference to final, with the human check marked at every stage.
4. Reference against output. The client's product image on the left, the generated frame on the right: [what matched, what was corrected].
5. Rejected take. Why this shot was dropped: [reason, for example the piece changed shape mid-shot].
6. Shot list. Five or six held shots, each with its length in seconds.
7. Grade comparison. Raw generated clip beside the graded one: [what the grade fixed].
8. Final frame. The closing shot, held for [N] seconds.

RESULT
[Views] views and [saves] saves, from the brand's campaign report for [dates, platform]. How the numbers were counted: [definition of a view and a save, as given in the report]. Client feedback, shared with permission: "[quote from the client's written feedback]."

REFLECTION
What I would do differently: [one specific thing, for example start the reference library on day one rather than day three]. The lesson I took away: decide on day one what must not change, and build the pipeline around that.

HUMAN CONTRIBUTION AND CREDITS
Art direction and the generation pipeline: me. [Name], [role]. [Name], [role]. [Name], [role]. The jewellery designs belong to the client. Brand name withheld under NDA.

samples.text:
PRD: UPI AutoPay mandate setup for monthly memberships

Owner: [PM name]
Status: Draft v0.1
Last updated: [date]
Reviewers: two engineers, designer, QA, studio-operations lead
Links: designs [design link], tickets [ticket link], payment provider docs [link]

Terms used in this document:
Member: a person with a monthly membership.
Mandate: a UPI AutoPay instruction a member authorises in their UPI app, so the studio can debit the monthly fee.
Renewal date: the day the membership fee falls due.

1. PROBLEM AND CONTEXT
Members renew their monthly membership by hand each month. When they forget, the membership lapses [consequence for the member, as the client defines it]. The client's data shows [X]% of members lapsed in at least one month in [period], and [Y]% of those lapsed members did not return within [N] days (client's renewal records, [date range]). [If the client supplies it: staff time spent chasing renewals each month.]

We want members to set up a UPI AutoPay mandate once, inside the renewal flow, so the fee is debited on the renewal date without a manual step. Why now: [reason supplied by the client, for example a renewal target for the next quarter].

2. GOALS AND SUCCESS METRICS
| Goal | Metric | Baseline | Target | How measured |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fewer lapses | Members whose membership lapses for any day after the renewal date, as a share of members due | [X]% | [Y]% within [N] months of launch | Renewal records, monthly |
| Adoption | Members renewing in a month who have an active mandate | 0% (no mandate exists today) | [Z]% within [60] days of launch | Mandate status table |
| Setup works | Mandate setups completed as a share of setups started | Not available (new flow) | At least [N]% | In-app events, weekly |

Guardrail: billing-related support tickets per month must not rise above [N] after launch (baseline [N], support log).

3. NON-GOALS
- AutoPay for class packs, drop-in bookings or any one-time payment.
- Other recurring methods (cards, e-NACH) in this release.
- Any change to membership prices, discounts or refund rules.
- A new billing-history screen. Members see mandate status only.
- Changes to how invoices are generated.

4. USERS AND USE CASES
Primary user: the member renewing a monthly membership. Secondary user: the studio-operations lead, who follows up on failed mandates.
1. As a member, I want to set up AutoPay once, so my membership does not lapse when I forget.
2. As a member, I want to see what will be charged, when and how to stop it before I authorise, so there are no surprises.
3. As a member whose debit failed, I want to know why and what to do, so I can still renew.
4. As a member, I want to cancel AutoPay without contacting the studio.
5. As the studio-operations lead, I want to see which members have active, failed or cancelled mandates, so I can follow up.

5. REQUIREMENTS
Priority: M = must, S = should, C = could.
R1 (M) The renewal screen offers "Set up AutoPay" next to "Pay once". Acceptance: both options show for every member with a monthly plan, and "Pay once" still works as today.
R2 (M) Before the member authorises, the screen shows the amount in rupees, the debit day each month and how to cancel. Acceptance: all three appear on the same screen as the authorise button.
R3 (M) The member authorises the mandate in their UPI app. The app opens the UPI intent with the correct amount and frequency. Acceptance: on a test account, the mandate appears in the UPI app with a monthly frequency and the studio's name.
R4 (M) The app stores the mandate reference, status, amount, frequency and next debit date. It does not store the member's UPI PIN or bank details. Acceptance: a database review shows no such fields.
R5 (M) After successful authorisation, the member sees a confirmation with the next debit date. Acceptance: the date matches the stored next debit date.
R6 (M) On the renewal date, the studio initiates the debit and updates the membership when the payment succeeds. Acceptance: in the test environment the membership extends by one month within [N] minutes of a successful debit.
R7 (M) Failure state, mandate rejected. If the member declines, or the UPI app returns a failure, the member returns to the renewal screen. The screen says the mandate was not set up and that "Pay once" is available. Acceptance: no mandate record is created in status "active".
R8 (M) Failure state, debit declined. If the bank declines a debit, the member keeps access for [N] days and receives a message with a "Pay once" link. The mandate stays active for the next cycle unless the bank cancels it. Acceptance: the membership shows "payment due", not "lapsed", until day [N].
R9 (M) Failure state, member cancels in their UPI app. The studio marks the mandate "cancelled" within [24 hours] of the payment partner's notification. The member is then prompted to pay once for the next cycle. Acceptance: the status changes in a test after a revoke.
R10 (M) The AutoPay screens and messages collect only what is needed to run the mandate, say so in plain words, and do not add the member to marketing lists. Acceptance: no marketing flag is changed by setting up a mandate.
R11 (S) The member can cancel AutoPay in the app from the membership screen. Acceptance: cancellation revokes the mandate with the payment partner, and the status shows "cancelled".
R12 (S) The studio-operations lead sees mandate status for each member in the admin view. Acceptance: filter by active, failed or cancelled returns the correct count against the test data.
R13 (S) The member receives a notification about each debit result. Acceptance: one message per debit; channels as decided in Open question 3.
R14 (S) The app shows a message that the member's bank or UPI app sends its own advance notice before each debit. Acceptance: copy appears on the confirmation screen.
R15 (C) A member who sets up AutoPay while a manual payment is pending is not charged twice. Acceptance: in a test, only one successful payment is recorded per renewal date.

6. UX AND FLOWS
Designs: [design link]. States to be designed: happy path, empty (no mandate), loading, rejected, bank declined, cancelled, permission denied, and a time-out where the UPI app does not return.

7. CONSTRAINTS, ASSUMPTIONS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Depends on the payment provider's UPI AutoPay support: [provider name and API version].
- The RBI framework for recurring payments requires the customer's bank or UPI app to send a notice before each debit and limits transactions without extra authentication to a set amount. Assumption: the membership fee is within that limit [engineering to confirm with the provider].
- Assumption: mandate status callbacks arrive reliably. To validate in the test environment.
- Timeline: [launch date supplied by the client].

8. LAUNCH PLAN
1. Internal test with staff accounts behind a feature flag.
2. [5]% of members for [2] weeks.
3. [25]% for [2] weeks, then 100%.
4. Support: help article and a front-desk script by the studio-operations lead before step 2.
5. Rollback trigger: setup success below [N]% for 24 hours, or billing tickets above [N] a week. Turn the flag off.

9. OPEN QUESTIONS
1. What is the grace period after a failed debit? Owner: studio-operations lead. Due: [date].
2. Is the membership fee within the no-extra-authentication limit with our provider? Owner: engineer 1. Due: [date].
3. Which channels send the debit result: push, SMS, email? Owner: PM with designer. Due: [date].
4. Do we need legal review of the consent wording? Owner: PM. Due: [date].
5. Does the provider support a "retry once" on a declined debit? Owner: engineer 2. Due: [date].
